item.title: A Chemist's Glossary of Neural Network and GNN Training Terms
item.description:
The words in a training script are the steps of one loop. An epoch, a batch, a loss, and a scaffold split are not four topics. They are where you are in that loop, and what you are allowed to look at while you are there.

This note is the vocabulary. The and the are the hands-on graph code. The is how those models arrived in drug discovery. The and the are why the split decides whether a good number means anything.

Epoch, batch, iteration

Epoch. One complete pass of the training set through the model. Twenty epochs means every training molecule is seen twenty times. Seeing a molecule again is the point: the first pass rarely fits a nonlinear model.

Batch, or mini-batch. The subset processed together before the weights change. A batch of 32 molecular graphs is one input to the forward pass, not 32 separate trainings.

Batch size. How many samples are in that subset. It is a hyperparameter. It is not learned.

Iteration, or step. One trip around the top row of Figure 1. One batch in, one weight update out. An epoch is a pile of iterations.

Learning rate. How far the optimizer moves each weight. Too large and the loss jumps or diverges. Too small and the same epoch count barely moves the fit.

Weights, or parameters. The numbers inside the model that training changes. In a GNN the matrices that transform atom features at each layer are weights. They start random. A seed makes that start repeatable.

Hyperparameters. Choices fixed before training: learning rate, batch size, depth, hidden size, dropout. They are not updated by loss.backward().

Activation. A nonlinear function after a layer. Without it, stacking layers is still one linear map. ReLU replaces negative values with zero and leaves positive values alone. It is a common choice, not a law.

Gradient. How the loss changes if one weight is nudged. Backpropagation computes one gradient per weight [1]. A large positive gradient means increasing that weight would increase the loss, so the optimizer moves the other way.

Forward, loss, backward, step

Forward pass. The batch goes through the model and comes out as predictions. For a regression GNN that is one predicted pIC50 per molecule. The model does not know that a higher pIC50 is more potent. It is fitting the number you handed it.

Loss. One number that says how wrong those predictions are. Training minimizes it. A lower training loss means a closer fit to the training labels, including whatever noise is in them.

Mean squared error. The average squared gap between prediction and target.

$$ \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 $$

Suppose three pIC50 values are 5, 5, and 5, and the model says 5, 5, and 8. The errors are 0, 0, and 3. MSE is $(0 + 0 + 9) / 3 = 3$. The one miss dominates because the error was squared. That is why MSE is a common default for pIC50 or solubility, and why a few bad labels can steer it.

Mean absolute error. The average of the absolute gaps, $|y - \hat{y}|$. On the same three points it is $(0 + 0 + 3) / 3 = 1$. The outlier still hurts, but it is not squared. MAE is the loss to reach for when a few noisy assays should not run the fit.

Binary cross-entropy. The loss for a yes/no label. The model offers a probability of “active”, and the loss compares it with 0 or 1. Some implementations want that probability. PyTorch’s BCEWithLogitsLoss wants the raw score and applies the sigmoid itself. Mixing those two double-applies the sigmoid.

Categorical cross-entropy. The same idea for more than two exclusive classes. One compound, one class, a predicted distribution over the classes.

Backward pass. The gradient of that one loss number is computed for every weight, by the chain rule run from the loss back to the inputs [1]. In PyTorch, loss.backward() does this. It adds the new gradients onto whatever is already stored.

Optimizer step. The optimizer turns those gradients into a change in the weights. optimizer.step() does that. optimizer.zero_grad() has to come first. Skip it and the second batch’s update still contains the first batch’s gradient.

Loss is not the metric

The loss is what the optimizer sees. A metric is what you use to decide the model is worth keeping. They are often different functions, and the metric has to be computed on molecules the weights did not train on. The is that rule in full.

Accuracy. The fraction of labels that match. It is a bad compass on a screen. If 95 of 100 compounds are inactive, predicting “inactive” for all of them scores 0.95 and finds no active.

Precision. Of the compounds called active, the fraction that are active. Precision 0.90 means most of the shortlist is real. The cost of a false active is a synthesis or a purchase that fails.

Recall. Of the true actives, the fraction the model names. Recall 0.10 with precision 0.90 is a careful model that misses almost everything.

F1. The harmonic mean of precision and recall:

$$ F_1 = \frac{2PR}{P + R}. $$

With $P = 0.90$ and $R = 0.10$, the ordinary average is 0.50 and $F_1 = 0.18$. The harmonic mean refuses to be impressed by one of the two being high.

For regression the usual reported numbers are RMSE, MAE, and $R^2$. RMSE is the square root of MSE, in the same units as pIC50. $R^2$ compares the errors with the errors of predicting the training mean. It is not a percent correct.

Optimizers

Optimizer. The rule that converts gradients into the step.

SGD. Subtract learning rate times the mini-batch gradient from each weight. Often used with momentum, which keeps a running average of recent gradients so one noisy batch does not reverse the step.

RMSProp. Gives each weight its own step size from a running average of squared gradients. Useful when some weights see huge gradients and others see tiny ones.

Adam. Momentum and a per-weight step size together [2]. It is a common default for GNNs because it often trains without a long search over the learning rate. “Often” is not “for every dataset”.

Learning-rate scheduler. A rule that changes the learning rate as training goes. A typical one lowers it after the validation loss has stalled.

When training goes wrong

Overfitting. Training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises. The model is fitting the training set’s noise. Early stopping, dropout, weight decay, or more diverse molecules are the usual responses. A bigger model is not.

Underfitting. Both losses stay high. The model is too small, the training is too short, or the learning rate is too low to move.

Dropout. During training, a random fraction of the activations is set to zero, so the network cannot depend on one path [3]. At evaluation that randomness is turned off. In PyTorch, model.train() uses dropout and model.eval() disables it. Scoring the validation set in train mode makes the number noisy for no reason.

Weight decay. A penalty on large weights, the L2 penalty, set with weight_decay on most PyTorch optimizers. It is not the same knob as dropout. Dropout hits activations. Weight decay hits the parameters.

Normalization. Putting numbers on a stable scale. Standardizing the input descriptors, or the pIC50 values, is the chemist’s version. Batch normalization does a related rescaling inside the network, using the mean and variance of the current batch [4]. Because that mean depends on the batch, batch normalization also cares about train() versus eval().

Early stopping. Stop when validation performance has not improved for a set number of epochs, and keep the weights from the best epoch, not the last one.

Seed. A random seed fixes the split, the initial weights, the shuffle, and the dropout masks. One seed makes a run repeatable. It does not make the number typical. The is that argument in full.

Tuning, on the right set

Grid search. Every combination from a short list. Three learning rates and three batch sizes are nine trainings.

Random search. Draw combinations from ranges. Bergstra and Bengio showed that, for the same number of trainings, random search beats a grid when only a few of the hyperparameters actually matter [5].

Bayesian optimization. Fit a model of how the validation score depends on the hyperparameters, and use it to pick the next trial [6]. It earns its cost when one training run is expensive.

All three read the validation score. Using the test score to pick a learning rate turns the test set into a second validation set. The number you then “report” has already been used to choose the model.

Graphs, in the same loop

Nothing above changes when the input is a graph. The forward pass does.

Graph. Nodes and edges. For a molecule the usual choice is atoms as nodes and bonds as edges. Ethanol drawn without hydrogens is three nodes and two edges, C–C–O. Including hydrogens is a different graph and a different model.

Node features. The vector on each atom: element, formal charge, aromaticity, hybridization, hydrogen count. The network does not see the periodic table except through this vector.

Edge features. The vector on each bond: order, conjugation, ring membership.

Message passing. A node builds a new vector from its own features and its neighbors’ features. Gilmer and colleagues put a large family of molecular GNNs into this one pattern [7]. After one round, a carbon’s vector contains information about the atoms bonded to it, and nothing further.

Aggregation. How the neighbors’ messages become one vector: sum, mean, or max. Sum can tell a carbon with three neighbors from a carbon with one. Mean divides that difference out.

Depth. The number of message-passing layers. Each layer adds one bond of reach. Three layers mean an atom can be influenced by atoms three bonds away, not by the whole molecule.

Oversmoothing. As layers repeat, the node vectors move toward each other and become less useful as a description of one atom [8]. When a deeper GNN gets worse, this is one of the first suspects, ahead of “needs more epochs”.

Readout, or pooling. The step that turns every atom vector into one molecule vector, often by a sum or a mean. A molecular property such as pIC50 is predicted from that vector, not from a single atom. The is where readout sits in a DGL model.

Splits

Training, validation, and test. Train on the training set. Choose hyperparameters and the stopping epoch on the validation set. Touch the test set once, at the end. An 80/10/10 cut is a common starting point, not a justified one. The separates internal fit, cross-validation, and an external check.

Random split. Each molecule is assigned independently. Close analogues of a test compound usually land in training. The model can look strong by recognizing a near neighbor.

Scaffold split. Molecules are grouped by core, and a whole core goes to one side. MoleculeNet’s split uses the Bemis–Murcko scaffold so that the test molecules are new chemotypes relative to training [9]. The Chemprop paper evaluates property models on that kind of split as well as on a random one [10]. It is harder, and it is closer to “would this work on a series we have not made”.

Data leakage. Anything from the evaluation molecules that is allowed to influence training. A near-duplicate compound is the obvious case. The same protein, or a label derived from the test rows, is the less obvious one. The is a laptop-scale check of how large that effect is for one GNN, and when it is not.

Regression target. A continuous label: pIC50, logS, a computed free energy. State the units.

Classification target. A class, often active or inactive at a potency cutoff. The cutoff is part of the model. A different cutoff is a different dataset, and it changes precision and recall even when the molecules do not change.

The loop in PyTorch

The sketch below is the top row of Figure 1, then the validation step. MyModel and the two loaders are stand-ins. DGL and PyTorch Geometric supply loaders that batch graphs into one disconnected graph. The order of the seven calls does not change.

import torch

model = MyModel()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-5)
loss_fn = torch.nn.MSELoss()

for epoch in range(20):
 model.train()
 for x, y in train_loader:
 optimizer.zero_grad()
 pred = model(x)
 loss = loss_fn(pred, y)
 loss.backward()
 optimizer.step()

 model.eval()
 with torch.no_grad():
 totals = [loss_fn(model(x), y).item() for x, y in val_loader]
 val_loss = sum(totals) / len(totals)
 print(f"epoch {epoch + 1}: validation loss {val_loss:.3f}")

torch.no_grad() stops PyTorch from storing the graph of operations it would need for a backward pass. Evaluation does not take a step, so that graph is wasted memory. The printed val_loss averages one number per batch, so a final batch of 8 counts as much as a batch of 32. A mean over molecules weights each compound once. Either is fine if you say which one you plotted.

Cheat sheet

Term In one line
Epoch One full pass over the training set
Batch, batch size Samples per update, and how many
Iteration One weight update
Learning rate Size of that update
Weights The numbers training changes
Hyperparameters The numbers you set before training
Activation The nonlinearity after a layer
Gradient How the loss moves if one weight moves
Forward pass Batch in, predictions out
Loss The number being minimized
Backward pass Gradients by the chain rule
Optimizer step Weights updated from those gradients
MSE, MAE Squared error, absolute error
Cross-entropy Classification loss
Accuracy Fraction correct; hollow if one class dominates
Precision, recall, F1 Shortlist quality, actives found, and their balance
SGD, RMSProp, Adam Three common optimizers
Scheduler Changes the learning rate on a schedule
Overfitting Training fit improves, new molecules get worse
Dropout Random activations dropped, and only while training
Weight decay Penalty on large weights
Normalization A stable scale for inputs or for a layer
Early stopping Keep the best epoch, not the last
Seed Makes one run repeatable
Grid, random, Bayesian Three ways to search hyperparameters
Graph Atoms as nodes, bonds as edges
Node and edge features The vectors the GNN is allowed to see
Message passing A node rewritten from its neighbors
Aggregation Sum, mean, or max of those messages
Depth One layer, one bond of reach
Oversmoothing Deeper layers, less distinct atoms
Readout Atom vectors to one molecule vector
Train, validation, test Fit, choose, report once
Scaffold split A new core in the test set
Data leakage Evaluation information reaching training
Regression, classification A pIC50, or a cutoff called active

References

  1. Rumelhart DE, Hinton GE, Williams RJ. Learning representations by back-propagating errors. Nature 1986;323:533–536. doi:
  2. Kingma DP, Ba J. Adam: a method for stochastic optimization. arXiv:1412.6980.
  3. Srivastava N, Hinton G, Krizhevsky A, Sutskever I, Salakhutdinov R. Dropout: a simple way to prevent neural networks from overfitting. J Mach Learn Res 2014;15:1929–1958.
  4. Ioffe S, Szegedy C. Batch normalization: accelerating deep network training by reducing internal covariate shift. arXiv:1502.03167.
  5. Bergstra J, Bengio Y. Random search for hyper-parameter optimization. J Mach Learn Res 2012;13:281–305.
  6. Snoek J, Larochelle H, Adams RP. Practical Bayesian optimization of machine learning algorithms. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 25, 2012. arXiv:1206.2944.
  7. Gilmer J, Schoenholz SS, Riley PF, Vinyals O, Dahl GE. Neural message passing for quantum chemistry. Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 70, 2017.
  8. Li Q, Han Z, Wu XM. Deeper insights into graph convolutional networks for semi-supervised learning. AAAI 2018. arXiv:1801.07606.
  9. Wu Z, Ramsundar B, Feinberg EN, Gomes J, Geniesse C, Pappu AS, Leswing K, Pande V. MoleculeNet: a benchmark for molecular machine learning. Chem Sci 2018;9:513–530. doi:
  10. Yang K, Swanson K, Jin W, Coley C, Eiden P, Gao H, Guzman-Perez A, Hopper T, Kelley B, Mathea M, Palmer A, Settels V, Jaakkola T, Jensen K, Barzilay R. Analyzing learned molecular representations for property prediction. J Chem Inf Model 2019;59:3370–3388. doi:

item.title: A History of Graph Neural Networks in Drug Discovery
item.description:
The graph was already the model. ECFP hashed a neighborhood. A GNN learns the neighborhood. The later step, the one that changes a binding model, is putting the protein in the same graph and then refusing to trust a single pose.

Graphs before they were learned

A molecule is a graph: atoms as nodes, bonds as edges. ECFP and Morgan fingerprints, and a lot of QSAR descriptors, hash a local neighborhood into a fixed vector. Graph kernels did the same job with a hand-built similarity, before message passing was trained.

Protein–ligand models already built interaction graphs. A ligand atom or a residue linked to a protein residue if they were in contact, and a summary of that graph went into a classical model. The graph was a feature recipe. It was not trained end to end.

Ligand graphs, mid-2010s

Message passing, graph convolution, and graph attention made the graph the input. The first drug-discovery use was ligand-only: solubility, toxicity, activity, ADMET. The model learned embeddings and passed them along bonds. For several years that was what “a GNN for drug discovery” meant. The protein, if it appeared, arrived as a sequence or a profile, or not at all.

The complex is the graph

The shift is to treat the complex as one object.

  • Two graphs, protein and ligand, plus edges between residues and atoms inside a distance cutoff.
  • One graph of both atom sets, with edges for contacts, distances, and interaction types.
  • Message passing that crosses those edges, so the 3D arrangement is part of the update.

The site is then learnable. Hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic contacts, and metal coordination can be edge labels. Attention decides which of them matter.

Geometry and attention

Three habits stuck.

Distances, radial basis functions, or an SE(3)-equivariant layer keep the coordinates and the symmetry. The model starts to look like a scoring function with trained parameters.

Edges stop meaning only “bonded” or “within some angstrom cutoff.” They carry the interaction class. A cytochrome is the example in this note: iron coordination and a few C–H distances dominate the mechanism, so an edge label is the natural place for them.

GAT-style attention weights the neighbors. Attentive pooling, or multiple-instance learning over poses, pockets, and conformers, chooses which part of a messy input to trust.

Poses as a bag

Docking and MD return an ensemble. The pipeline this note describes:

  1. One protein–ligand graph per pose, with an edge-aware GAT such as EdgeGATConv.
  2. A readout to one embedding per pose.
  3. Attention-based MIL (ABMIL) pools those embeddings and learns which poses matter for binding or for substrate classification.
  4. The prediction is made from that pooled vector.

The docking score is no longer the only way to pick a pose. The model can learn what a productive pose looks like, and it can also learn to ignore the rest.

Fingerprints made the graph implicit. Ligand GNNs made it trained. Complex graphs added the site. Equivariant layers tied the result to geometry. MIL is the step that stops pretending one frame was the complex.

item.title: Getting Started with Graph Neural Networks for Protein–Ligand Complexes Using DGL
item.description:
A fingerprint collapses a docked complex to a fixed vector. A graph keeps the atoms, the bonds, and the contacts, and a GNN learns from that neighborhood. is the PyTorch library this note uses. The code below is the path from an empty graph to a label. Readout and, for a set of poses, the bag come after message passing.

The rest is the DGL user-guide path, in the language of a protein–ligand complex. No prior GNN course is assumed.

Why Graphs for Molecules?

A molecule has a natural graph structure. Atoms are nodes, bonds are edges. When you extend this to a protein–ligand complex, you can add edges for non-covalent contacts (hydrogen bonds, hydrophobic interactions, π-stacking) connecting ligand atoms to binding-pocket residues.

The key advantage: a GNN can aggregate information from a node’s neighborhood iteratively, so after a few layers, each atom’s representation encodes not just its own identity but the chemical context around it. This is exactly what a human medicinal chemist does mentally when reading a 2D structure.

The DGL Core: DGLGraph

Everything in DGL revolves around the DGLGraph object. Think of it as a PyTorch-native container for graph-structured data.

import dgl
import torch

# Define edges as (source_nodes, destination_nodes)
src = torch.tensor([0, 0, 1, 2])
dst = torch.tensor([1, 2, 2, 3])

g = dgl.graph((src, dst))
print(g)
# Graph(num_nodes=4, num_edges=4, ndata_schemes={}, edata_schemes={})

For molecular graphs, edges are usually undirected (bond A→B is the same as B→A), so use dgl.to_bidirected():

g = dgl.to_bidirected(g)

Attaching Features

Node and edge features are stored as PyTorch tensors directly on the graph:

# Node features: e.g., one-hot atomic number, partial charge, aromaticity...
g.ndata['feat'] = torch.randn(g.num_nodes(), 32)

# Edge features: e.g., bond type, interatomic distance...
g.edata['dist'] = torch.randn(g.num_edges(), 1)

This is the bridge between your cheminformatics featurization pipeline (RDKit, MDAnalysis, etc.) and the GNN. Whatever features you compute, just stick them in ndata or edata.

Heterogeneous Graphs: Protein + Ligand Together

If you want to model protein–ligand contacts explicitly (not just the ligand in isolation), DGL supports heterogeneous graphs: graphs with multiple node and edge types.

g = dgl.heterograph({
 ('ligand_atom', 'bond', 'ligand_atom'): (lig_src, lig_dst),
 ('ligand_atom', 'contacts', 'protein_residue'): (lig_ids, res_ids),
 ('protein_residue', 'contacts', 'ligand_atom'): (res_ids, lig_ids),
})

g.nodes['ligand_atom'].data['feat'] = ligand_atom_features
g.nodes['protein_residue'].data['feat'] = residue_features

This is a more faithful representation of the complex: the network can learn that certain binding-pocket residues modulate the ligand’s representation depending on how they interact.

Message Passing: How GNNs Actually Work

This is the heart of DGL and the heart of every GNN. Message passing works in two steps per layer:

Step 1: Edge-wise (messages): For each edge, compute a “message” from the source node’s features (and optionally the edge’s own features).

Step 2: Node-wise (aggregation + update): Each node collects all incoming messages, aggregates them (sum, mean, or max), and updates its own features.

Mathematically, for node v at layer t+1:

$$h_v^{(t+1)} = \psi\!\left(h_v^{(t)},\ \rho\!\left(\left\{ \phi(h_u^{(t)}, h_v^{(t)}, w_{uv}) : u \in \mathcal{N}(v) \right\}\right)\right)$$

where φ is the message function, ρ is the aggregation (e.g., mean), and ψ is the update function.

In DGL code, the fastest way uses built-in functions:

import dgl.function as fn

# Message: copy source node feature → edge mailbox
# Reduce: average all incoming messages → update node feature
g.update_all(fn.copy_u('h', 'm'), fn.mean('m', 'h'))

This runs as fused CUDA kernels, much faster than writing Python loops.

For custom behavior (e.g., distance-weighted messages):

def weighted_message(edges):
 # edges.src['h']: source node features
 # edges.data['dist']: edge distance
 return {'m': edges.src['h'] * torch.exp(-edges.data['dist'])}

g.update_all(weighted_message, fn.sum('m', 'h'))

Built-in GNN Layers

DGL ships with ready-to-use layers in dgl.nn.pytorch. The most useful for molecular tasks:

Layer When to use
GraphConv Simplest baseline, no edge features
GATConv Learns per-edge attention weights; great for contacts with varying importance
NNConv Edge-feature-conditioned messages; use when bond type or distance matters
HeteroGraphConv Wraps per-relation convolutions for heterogeneous graphs

A simple two-layer GAT:

import dgl.nn.pytorch as dglnn
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class MolGNN(nn.Module):
 def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden_dim):
 super().__init__()
 self.gat1 = dglnn.GATConv(in_dim, hidden_dim, num_heads=4)
 self.gat2 = dglnn.GATConv(hidden_dim * 4, hidden_dim, num_heads=1)

 def forward(self, g, feat):
 h = F.elu(self.gat1(g, feat).flatten(1)) # (N, hidden*4)
 h = self.gat2(g, h).squeeze(1) # (N, hidden)
 return h

Graph-Level Prediction: Readout

After message passing, each node has a learned embedding. For a graph-level prediction (e.g., is this compound active?), you need to compress the variable-number of node embeddings into a single fixed-size vector. This is called readout.

DGL provides built-in readout functions:

# Mean of all node features → one vector per graph
graph_embedding = dgl.mean_nodes(g, 'h')

# Also available: dgl.sum_nodes, dgl.max_nodes

For a batch of graphs (many compounds at once):

bg = dgl.batch([g1, g2, g3, ...]) # one disconnected super-graph
# ... run message passing on bg ...
embeddings = dgl.mean_nodes(bg, 'h') # shape (batch_size, hidden_dim)

dgl.batch() is what makes mini-batch training efficient: DGL treats the batch as a single large graph (with no edges between the individual molecules), runs all convolutions in one GPU call, then recovers per-graph embeddings with readout.

The Full Graph Classification Pipeline

Putting it all together: a classifier that takes a molecule graph and outputs a binary label:

import dgl
import dgl.nn.pytorch as dglnn
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class GraphClassifier(nn.Module):
 def __init__(self, in_dim, hidden_dim, n_classes=2):
 super().__init__()
 self.conv1 = dglnn.GATConv(in_dim, hidden_dim, num_heads=4)
 self.conv2 = dglnn.GATConv(hidden_dim * 4, hidden_dim, num_heads=1)
 self.classify = nn.Linear(hidden_dim, n_classes)

 def forward(self, g, feat):
 # Message passing
 h = F.elu(self.conv1(g, feat).flatten(1))
 h = self.conv2(g, h).squeeze(1)

 # Store updated features
 with g.local_scope():
 g.ndata['h'] = h
 # Readout: mean over all atoms → graph embedding
 graph_feat = dgl.mean_nodes(g, 'h')

 return self.classify(graph_feat)


# Training loop sketch
model = GraphClassifier(in_dim=32, hidden_dim=64)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

for epoch in range(100):
 for batched_graphs, labels in dataloader:
 feats = batched_graphs.ndata['feat']
 logits = model(batched_graphs, feats)
 loss = loss_fn(logits, labels)
 optimizer.zero_grad()
 loss.backward()
 optimizer.step()

Building a Dataset

DGL has a dataset API that handles caching processed graphs to disk, important when building graphs from PDB/SDF files is slow.

class MolDataset(dgl.data.DGLDataset):
 def __init__(self, raw_dir):
 super().__init__(name='mol_dataset', raw_dir=raw_dir)

 def process(self):
 self.graphs, self.labels = [], []
 for path in self._get_files():
 g, label = self._build_graph(path) # your featurization here
 self.graphs.append(g)
 self.labels.append(label)

 def __getitem__(self, i):
 return self.graphs[i], self.labels[i]

 def __len__(self):
 return len(self.graphs)

 def has_cache(self):
 return os.path.exists(self.save_path)

 def save(self):
 dgl.save_graphs(self.save_path, self.graphs,
 {'labels': torch.tensor(self.labels)})

 def load(self):
 self.graphs, label_dict = dgl.load_graphs(self.save_path)
 self.labels = label_dict['labels'].tolist()

Pair this with a DataLoader using dgl.dataloading.GraphDataLoader (or PyTorch’s standard DataLoader with a custom collate_fn that calls dgl.batch()).

Multiple Instances per Compound: the Bag Approach

A common scenario in ensemble docking: you dock one compound against N different receptor conformations and get N poses, each a separate graph. You want to make one prediction per compound, not one per pose.

This is a natural fit for Multiple Instance Learning (MIL). The trick with DGL:

def predict_bag(model, bag_of_graphs):
 # Stack all N pose-graphs into one batched graph
 bg = dgl.batch(bag_of_graphs)
 feats = bg.ndata['feat']

 # Run GNN - poses stay disconnected (no cross-pose edges)
 h = model.encode(bg, feats) # node embeddings

 with bg.local_scope():
 bg.ndata['h'] = h
 pose_embeds = dgl.mean_nodes(bg, 'h') # (N, h_dim) - one per pose

 # MIL aggregation over the bag
 bag_embed = pose_embeds.mean(0, keepdim=True) # mean pooling
 return model.classify(bag_embed)

The key insight: dgl.batch() keeps the poses structurally independent (no edges cross between them), so the GNN respects the fact that each pose is a separate physical structure. The MIL aggregation then decides how to combine them for the final prediction.

For a more expressive aggregation, use attention MIL:

class AttentionMIL(nn.Module):
 def __init__(self, h_dim):
 super().__init__()
 self.attention = nn.Sequential(
 nn.Linear(h_dim, 64),
 nn.Tanh(),
 nn.Linear(64, 1)
 )

 def forward(self, pose_embeds): # (N, h_dim)
 scores = self.attention(pose_embeds) # (N, 1)
 weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=0)
 return (weights * pose_embeds).sum(0) # (h_dim,)

Attention MIL has a nice bonus: weights tells you which poses contributed most to the prediction, interpretable by design.

Which Chapters to Read First

If you’re using this post as a reading guide alongside the :

Priority Chapter Why
⭐⭐⭐ Ch 1.2–1.5: Graphs, features, heterograph Core data structure
⭐⭐⭐ Ch 2.1–2.2: Message passing API The computation engine
⭐⭐⭐ Ch 5.4: Graph classification Your prediction task
⭐⭐ Ch 3: GNN modules Ready-to-use layers
⭐⭐ Ch 4: Data pipeline Dataset + caching
⭐ Ch 6–8: Stochastic / distributed / mixed precision Only if dataset is huge

Summary

DGL wraps the complexity of graph-structured computation behind a clean PyTorch API. For molecular applications, the workflow is:

  1. Build a DGLGraph for each complex: atoms as nodes, bonds/contacts as edges, features from your cheminformatics toolkit
  2. Choose a GNN layer: GATConv is a strong default
  3. Run message passing: each atom aggregates information from its neighbors
  4. Apply readout (dgl.mean_nodes) to get a fixed-size graph embedding
  5. Feed into a standard MLP classifier

The library handles batching, GPU transfer, and efficient sparse operations under the hood. Once you get the featurization right, the training code looks almost identical to a standard PyTorch image classifier.
